title: CI/CD build system
brief: Every time a developer saves code to the shared repository, you build and test it. Thousands of developers do this all day, and release day brings a rush. Builds must start quickly, but idle build machines cost real money.

clarify.q: How long may a build wait to start?
clarify.a: Under a few minutes. Developers get impatient after about two.

clarify.q: What if one broken build keeps crashing the workers?
clarify.a: Stop retrying it after a few tries, set it aside and tell the author. It must not block anyone else.
Yes, for a month, in cheap storage.

clarify.q: May we use spare cheap machines that can disappear?
clarify.a: Yes. A build can be restarted if its machine vanishes.

notes: A build takes about 5 minutes and produces a 5 MB artifact. Convert peak batch arrivals into concurrent work.
A "batch" request here is one build job.

numbers.label: Builds started per second at peak
Builds running at once at peak
numbers.how: Little's law: 60 builds/s × 300 s (a 5-minute build) ≈ 18,000 running together, so real fleets autoscale thousands of runners (approx.)

numbers.label: Build artefacts stored
numbers.how: 800,000 builds a day × 5 MB × 30 days ≈ 120 TB (approx.)

hints: Builds arrive in bursts but workers cost money by the minute. How do you smooth that out?
Put a queue in front of the workers and let the worker count follow the queue. Plan for one bad job crashing a worker over and over.
Gateway, control servers, queue with a dead-letter queue, batch workers with autoscale, object storage for artefacts. Watch the queue with metrics and alerts.

editorial.summary: A push creates a job on a queue and the developer gets an instant answer. Build workers grow when the queue is long and shrink when it empties. Jobs that keep failing move to a dead-letter queue so one bad build cannot stall everybody.

designs.name: Queue with autoscaling workers
designs.why: The queue absorbs the release-day rush and the workers scale to match it. Dead-lettering stops a poison build from looping. Artefacts go to cheap object storage.

tradeoffs: Keeping a few workers warm starts builds faster but costs money all night.
Cheap interruptible machines save a lot but need builds that can restart safely.
A retry limit protects workers from a bad build. Without one a single job can occupy the whole fleet.
Longer artefact storage helps debugging but grows the monthly bill every day.
editorial.realWorld: Hosted build services run millions of jobs a day. Compute is billed per minute, a few tenths of a cent each for small machines (approx.).
